segments.title: AUKUS destroyer case starts with systems
segments.body: An AUKUS destroyer proposal raises the question of how one program could serve Australia, Britain, and the United States. NF-90 and Horizon provide examples for the criticism that multinational warship programs try to force different naval requirements into one ship. Hull steel costs less than the radars, missiles, weapons, computers, and other systems installed inside it. The proposed alternative is to develop those expensive systems as modules that each navy can assemble to suit its needs.

evidence.note: The question of expanding AUKUS to a destroyer or DDG serving all three partners.
NF-90 and Horizon as examples in the case for modular development of costly radars, weapons, and computers.

segments.summary: A proposed AUKUS destroyer partnership would share costly systems and weapons while leaving room for national hull designs.

segments.title: Hobart, Type 45, and Burke replacement pressure
segments.body: Hobart, Type 45, and Arleigh Burke illustrate the long interval between destroyer design decisions and operational ships. Hobart's Spanish parent design and Type 45's route through Horizon are traced to the breakup of NF-90. A planned service life of 25 to 30 years brings rising operating costs as a ship approaches replacement. Allowing roughly 15 years to deliver a British successor makes a 2026 start late against the 2036 date used here. The estimate of 2038 or later is a personal suspicion based on the pace of Type 26 construction, rather than a confirmed replacement schedule. The comparison treats Virginia, Astute, and Collins replacement needs as a precedent for collaboration across the three navies.

evidence.note: Hobart's Spanish parent design, Type 45's Horizon ancestry, and Arleigh Burke in the account of NF-90's breakup.
Planned service lives of 25 to 30 years, rising operating costs, an uncertain late-2030s replacement estimate, and the AUKUS submarine comparison.

segments.summary: AUKUS timing is tied to aging air-defense destroyers and the long lead time needed to replace Hobart, Type 45, and Burke-era ships.

segments.title: A Super Burke name for a redesigned successor
segments.body: High-volume Burke construction is credited with keeping unit prices reasonable, making a different ship difficult to justify against the established design. A partly humorous suggestion is to call a successor a Super Burke. The analogy is the Hornet name, with familiar branding helping Congress see continuity even if the interior is extensively redesigned. The imagined ship would look similar outside while supporting another 30 to 40 years of service. This is a proposed way to present a successor, rather than an existing program.

evidence.note: Burke production economies and the partly humorous Super Burke naming proposal, using the Hornet analogy for a substantially redesigned successor.

segments.summary: A partly humorous Super Burke proposal uses familiar branding to explain how a major internal redesign might retain political support.

segments.title: Pillar two links undersea autonomy and advanced technology
segments.body: Pillar two includes uncrewed undersea vessels that could take on some conventional-submarine duties. The proposed division of labor would let Australia's future nuclear submarines concentrate on their own roles while uncrewed vessels cover some tasks associated with Collins-class boats. Quantum technology is another area of work, with confidence that sustained investment will eventually produce results but no certainty about when. Cyber warfare completes this part of the technology survey. These examples give the destroyer proposal an existing setting for cooperation on systems.

evidence.note: Uncrewed undersea vessels taking on some conventional-submarine duties, followed by quantum technology's uncertain timetable.
Cyber warfare and changing public attention to advanced military technologies.

segments.summary: Uncrewed undersea vessels could assume some conventional-submarine tasks, while quantum technology and cyber warfare broaden AUKUS systems cooperation.

segments.title: Peer air defense must face layered threats
segments.body: Attention shifts between cyber warfare, hypersonic weapons, and cheap drones, but an older threat does not disappear when another attracts the headlines. A peer opponent is expected to combine different weapons if that offers an advantage. Cheap drones and fast cruise missiles could arrive alongside hypersonics in the same attack. The air-defense requirement in this argument is therefore to prepare for several threats at once. Treating each new weapon as a replacement for everything that came before would misread the problem.

evidence.note: A peer opponent is expected to combine cheap drones, fast cruise missiles, and probably hypersonics in the same attack.
Changing media attention does not mean that earlier threats have disappeared.

segments.summary: A peer opponent could combine cheap drones, fast cruise missiles, and hypersonic weapons in one attack.

segments.title: Fleet aging and procurement planning
segments.body: Fleet aging provides the basis for a sarcastic criticism of procurement planning across the AUKUS partners. Australian concern over the age of frigates and Collins-class submarines is contrasted with the known dates of their construction. Britain's carriers provide a related example: aircraft orders did not produce a mature air group from the outset. Congress supplies the funding example, with announced capabilities still requiring payment and organization. The criticism concerns governments treating foreseeable requirements as surprises.

evidence.note: A sarcastic criticism of surprise over Australian fleet age and British carrier air-group readiness.
A sarcastic funding example involving Congress and the organization needed to pay for announced capabilities.

segments.summary: A sarcastic procurement critique links Australian fleet aging, British carrier air groups, and American funding decisions to foreseeable requirements.

segments.title: A battleship cannot replace every Burke
segments.body: Repeated cancellations of Arleigh Burke successor programs form the background to the proposed Defiant battleship. The account connects the latest cancellation with that much larger ship. Calling Defiant a revived strike cruiser under a politically attractive battleship label is an interpretation of the proposal. Its size and expense are the reasons given for rejecting it as a one-for-one replacement for every Burke. A destroyer successor would still be needed in the force structure described here.

evidence.note: The canceled Burke-successor account and the interpretation of Defiant as a strike-cruiser idea presented as a battleship.
The proposed battleship's size and cost are the stated reasons it cannot replace every Burke.

segments.summary: The Defiant proposal is treated as too large and expensive to replace every Burke, leaving a separate destroyer requirement.

segments.title: VLS depth and design lock-in
segments.body: Hobart and Type 45 carry a 48-cell VLS inheritance linked here to NF-90's single-mission air-defense assumptions. Even the 96 cells of an Arleigh Burke are judged insufficient for the demand on modern missile magazines. Britain can sometimes pair two of its six Type 45s around a carrier, while Australia's three Hobarts offer less scope to do the same. Reopening a mature design to add capacity brings delay, which encourages navies to retain choices made much earlier. Type 45's power troubles provide a parallel criticism of specifying only enough margin for the original requirement. Linking missiles on other ships through shared sensors and data is acknowledged as useful, but the assessment is that it cannot substitute for replacing the Hobarts.

evidence.note: The 48-cell legacy attributed to NF-90, the 96-cell Burke comparison, limited design margins, fleet numbers, and the assessment that linked missiles on other ships cannot replace Hobarts.

segments.summary: The 48-cell legacy of NF-90 shows how early single-mission assumptions can lock later destroyers into inadequate magazine depth.

segments.title: Missile barges create an escort chain
segments.body: Uncrewed missile barges would need protection while traveling between their base and the force they support. Their missile cargo would make them targets for submarines, special forces, and other attackers, potentially requiring a warship escort. Empty vessels returning to reload would need replacements already available, so long transit distances increase the number of barges required. HMS Dragon's voyage from Britain toward Cyprus illustrates the effect of distance, fuel expenditure, and engine wear on transit speed. Faster passage also adds maintenance demand. Repeatedly deferring maintenance to surge ships is blamed for concentrating repair needs beyond the available dry-dock capacity, which had assumed more orderly maintenance schedules.

evidence.note: Escort vulnerability and the number of replacement missile barges needed during reloading voyages.
HMS Dragon's transit illustrates distance, fuel and engine-wear constraints, followed by deferred ship maintenance and insufficient dry-dock capacity.

segments.summary: Uncrewed missile carriers add magazine capacity only if a navy can protect, replace, fuel, and maintain the force that supports them.

segments.title: Type 83 and the danger of revolutionary promises
segments.body: Type 83's description as a system of systems prompts a concern about what the program intends to deliver. The phrase can describe a warship's complex computing, but its intended meaning in government language is questioned here. The accompanying promise of revolutionary development raises concerns about time, cost, and the risk of cancellation before the intended capability arrives. Harrier supplies the example: it is praised as a successful aircraft while also described as a stepping stone to a supersonic V/STOL successor that Britain never developed. That successor was intended to be faster and have longer range. The concern is that spending on an intermediate stage does not guarantee delivery of the later aircraft or warship originally envisaged.

evidence.note: Concerns about the meaning of Type 83's system-of-systems label and the time, cost, and cancellation risk of revolutionary development.
Harrier as an intermediate aircraft preceding an unrealized, faster, longer-range supersonic V/STOL successor.

segments.summary: Calling Type 83 a revolutionary system of systems raises the risk that Britain spends heavily on an ambition it later scales back or abandons.

segments.title: Institutional arguments for a shared destroyer project
segments.body: The proposed benefits of a shared destroyer effort extend to procurement institutions. Major allies are credited with helping keep British projects on an agreed course when domestic preferences change. An alliance design is also suggested as a possible route to US approval because it would begin as a joint project, rather than a foreign ship later adapted to American requirements. Australia could divide development costs with two partners while building ships domestically. Its investment in facilities for Type 26 construction is offered as a practical advantage for that approach.

evidence.note: Proposed institutional benefits for British and US procurement and shared Australian development costs using upgraded shipbuilding facilities.

segments.summary: The case for collaboration includes steadier British procurement, a possible route through US design approval, and shared Australian development costs.

segments.title: Submarine teams have more practice sharing designs
segments.body: The comparison of American design teams is a personal observation about collaboration. The surface community is described as treating Arleigh Burke standards as its reference point for new designs. Submarine designers have worked across Seawolf, several Virginia batches, Ohio, and Columbia, giving them experience with different designs. Joint British-American development of submarine missile-launch modules also required agreement on shared standards. That experience is offered as a reason submarine teams appear more accustomed to accommodating an external partner.

evidence.note: A personal observation about Burke-derived surface standards and greater adaptability among submarine designers.
Experience with several submarine designs and joint British-American development of missile-launch modules.

segments.summary: Experience with several submarine designs and shared British-American missile-launch modules underpins a personal comparison of US design cultures.

segments.title: Constellation shows how good requirements accumulate
segments.body: The Constellation procurement critique starts with two stated aims: Oliver Hazard Perry-like cost and construction efficiency, and the capability of a smaller Arleigh Burke. A proven foreign parent design was intended to make that combination attainable. Successive changes then applied additional American requirements and Burke-derived standards. The account links their accumulated cost, delay, and complexity to cancellation. It treats the individual decisions as well-intentioned while questioning their combined effect. The replacement ship is judged against Perry-level capability and described as falling below that personal baseline for a frigate.

evidence.note: Perry-like cost and construction efficiency combined with the desired capability of a smaller Burke using a proven foreign parent design.
Successive requirements add cost, time, and complexity in the cancellation account, followed by a personal assessment of the replacement's frigate capability.

segments.summary: The Constellation critique connects accumulated design changes with the loss of the cost and construction advantages sought from a proven parent frigate.

segments.title: SAMSON and SPY cooperation without radar uniformity
segments.body: A possible SAMSON-SPY arrangement would give SPY the long-range role handled by the second radar on Type 45. The idea comes from discussions heard about the two radar families, rather than a demonstrated installation. Their capabilities could complement each other, but electronic interference could also make integration difficult. Both systems have further improvements under way in the account given here. National radar development is then connected with the desire to retain some independent capability over a warship's long life. Common work on systems is presented alongside uncertainty about future relationships between partners.

evidence.note: Tentative complementary roles for SAMSON and SPY, including SPY's long-range role, possible electronic interference, and improvements to both radar families.
National system development and an uncertain future supply the reasoning for retaining some independent capability.

segments.summary: A tentative SAMSON-SPY combination raises questions about complementary radar roles, electronic interference, and continued national capability.

segments.title: Sovereign capability and supply-chain risk
segments.body: Multinational warship systems can create dependence as well as scale. Equipment sold under one national label may contain Italian, American, Swedish, British, or other components. Political and trade disputes can therefore affect spare parts and a navy's ability to maintain or use a system independently. Economies of scale still make multinational supply chains unavoidable because only a few firms may produce a specialized component. Cooperation can lower costs while the partners preserve key sovereign capabilities where practical.

evidence.note: Alliance dependence on supplies and spare parts in equipment containing components from several countries.
Supplier concentration driven by economies of scale and the suggested retention of some sovereign capability.

segments.summary: Equipment with one national brand can depend on components and spare parts from several countries, complicating independent support.

segments.title: Long ship lives connect generations of crews
segments.body: A warship commonly serves for 20 to 40 years, with some ships lasting 50 years. Its institutional history extends further through the people who train its first crew. Sailors trained aboard it later carry that experience into other ships. Following those connections backward and forward can cover roughly a century. This continuity explains the overlap between studying naval history and studying contemporary naval forces.

evidence.note: Ship service lives and successive generations of crew training connect roughly a century of naval experience.

segments.summary: A ship's service life and the crews trained before and after it connect present naval practice with a much longer institutional history.

segments.title: Different replacement calendars and the Burke production line
segments.body: The proposed arrangement separates American participation in AUKUS systems work from participation in a common ship. Continued US debate over battleships, cruisers, and destroyers is expected to delay a Burke-successor decision. Another decade of that debate is a personal forecast, not an announced schedule. Continued Burke construction is expected to provide ships during the interval. Australia and Britain are described as lacking the same production cushion, which explains the different replacement timetable assumed in this proposal.

evidence.note: The proposed separation of US hull participation from pillar-two systems work rests on a personal forecast of prolonged American ship-design debate.
Continued Burke production is expected to supply US ships during a delay that allied fleets cannot cover in the same way.

segments.summary: Continued Burke construction underlies a forecast that the US hull decision could take longer than allied replacement calendars allow.

segments.title: Destroyer replacement needs across prospective partners
segments.body: Japan has maintained a steady throughput of ships and is expected to need another destroyer design after its large Aegis system equipped vessels. Italy also appears in the proposed grouping alongside Australia and Britain. France is treated as a possible additional participant because of Horizon ancestry and a similar replacement timeline, with its nuclear-carrier and possible nuclear-escort discussions left as an unresolved difference. Strong air defense is a shared requirement in this comparison. Broader capability also matters: Type 26 and Type 31 illustrate ships with an emphasis on particular roles while retaining flexibility beyond them. Type 26's Royal Navy anti-submarine role is specifically distinguished from being exclusively an anti-submarine ship.

evidence.note: Japanese ship production and replacement needs, with France treated as a possible partner whose nuclear-escort discussions remain a qualification.
Strong air defense and multipurpose capability, with Type 26 and Type 31 illustrating an emphasis on one role without exclusive specialization.

segments.summary: Japan's production rhythm, France's possible nuclear-escort plans, and British frigate flexibility qualify the comparison of future destroyer requirements.

segments.title: Different industrial contributions to shared destroyer systems
segments.body: The proposed systems partnership draws on different areas of national development. Italy's contribution includes missile work through MBDA Italy and gun technology. Japan brings railguns, electronics, and power systems, while Britain brings gas turbines, radar, electronic warfare, and uncrewed systems. Australian work includes uncrewed vehicles and hypersonic missiles. Pooling this development effort is connected with an aspiration to put ships in the water in the mid-to-late 2030s, conditional on how the project is managed. The systems work is also identified as a possible contribution to AUKUS pillar two.

evidence.note: Italian, Japanese, British, and Australian areas of systems development.
Conditional mid-to-late-2030s ambition and a connection between shared systems development and AUKUS pillar two.

segments.summary: Missile, gun, radar, propulsion, and uncrewed-system work supplies the industrial context for a proposed shared development effort.

segments.title: Mission roles should determine national hulls
segments.body: National mission choices would shape hulls and superstructures even if the partners developed their systems together. Command teams need space that other ships may not require. Carrier protection, scouting, and surface-action-group work also place different demands on missile loadouts. An illustrative 128-cell arrangement divides its cells 64 and 64, with one half at strategic length. Another illustrative arrangement combines 48 strategic-length cells with 64 and 48 surface-to-air cells, giving 160 in total. These are examples worked through during the proposal, not settled specifications. They show how different balances of land-attack and air-defense weapons could use a shared set of systems.

evidence.note: Command-space requirements and carrier-escort, scouting, and surface-action roles create different hull and missile needs.
Illustrative 128-cell and 160-cell loadouts use different proportions of strategic-length and surface-to-air missile cells.

segments.summary: Shared combat systems can support different command spaces, hulls, and missile mixes for carrier escort, scouting, surface action, or land attack.

segments.title: Combat-system diversity creates dilemmas
segments.body: Aegis and SPY receive strong praise in the case for developing complementary radar and command systems. The concern is that universal use of one family would give an opponent a single technical target for countermeasures. Even a difficult system can receive concentrated study when there are no alternatives to prepare against. Several complementary systems would complicate that specialization. DragonFire and other national radar and weapons work provide examples of development that could contribute to this approach.

evidence.note: National weapons and radar work, followed by the concern that reliance on one combat-system family enables concentrated countermeasure development.

segments.summary: The case for complementary combat systems concerns an opponent's ability to concentrate countermeasure research on one radar and command-system family.

segments.title: How a submarine-only German fleet would change British deployments
segments.body: A hypothetical German fleet built entirely around submarines is used to explain the effect of having several different naval capabilities. In the counterfactual, Germany could not undertake the Norwegian operation as described, and Britain could concentrate its Atlantic response on anti-submarine warfare. Sloops and Flower-class corvettes would receive that emphasis while larger surface ships could shift toward the Mediterranean against Italy. Fleet-carrier anti-submarine patrols provide a related caution: early British use is described as contrary to the intended doctrine, undertaken because too few other carriers were available, and followed by a carrier loss. The example returns to the distinction between a single problem an opponent can concentrate on solving and several capabilities that impose competing demands.

evidence.note: Counterfactual submarine-only German fleet and the resulting British Atlantic and Mediterranean deployment choices.
Fleet-carrier anti-submarine patrol caution and the distinction between a single problem and competing demands.

segments.summary: A counterfactual German submarine-only fleet illustrates how removing surface threats could free British heavy ships for the Mediterranean.

segments.title: Combat information layout shapes the ship
segments.body: Joint work on radar and command information systems leads into the physical layout of a ship's command center. A Japanese design uses surrounding screens to help officers in the center understand the work of subordinate teams. The comparison with an early Aegis room concerns sightlines and information display, with the older desks making it difficult to see what other teams are handling. Modern warships are compared with floating data farms, using large amounts of computing in a saltwater environment. Their hardware is often a generation or two old by the time it becomes affordable to harden for naval service. Decisions about these systems influence the ship architecture that must accommodate them.

evidence.note: Joint command-system development, Japanese surrounding-screen layouts, and naval computers hardened for use in salt water.
An early Aegis room illustrates limited sightlines between desks and the influence of systems on ship architecture.

segments.summary: Japanese display concepts and early Aegis rooms show how command software, screens, and human sightlines become part of a warship's physical architecture.

segments.title: Power margin must cover climate and shortfalls
segments.body: The Type 45 example introduces two reasons for leaving reserve in a future ship's power generation. Electrical demand can increase, and installed equipment can operate less efficiently than expected. Systems in cold conditions need heating, while equipment in hotter regions needs additional cooling. Regular operations in the North and South Atlantic combined with occasional Gulf deployments illustrate a wide temperature range. High humidity around Japan supplies another operating condition. These differences explain why the proposal combines shared systems development with national responsibility for the ship that houses them.

evidence.note: Power-generation reserve for increasing demand and equipment operating less efficiently than expected.
Cold Atlantic conditions, Gulf heat, and Japanese humidity illustrate different national operating requirements.

segments.summary: Future destroyers need electrical and cooling reserve for growth, imperfect efficiency, and the climates in which each navy actually operates.

segments.title: Common aviation needs can shape different ships
segments.body: Shared aviation requirements could give otherwise different ships similar hangars and flight decks. The example uses two medium helicopters and three or four rotary UAVs for additional anti-submarine work and protection against small boats in narrow waters such as the Strait of Hormuz. Common handling needs would allow some design studies to be shared. National radar choices remain open: Britain and Italy might use indigenous systems, while Japan and Australia might retain SPY to avoid the cost of establishing another support chain. The command system would need to accommodate those choices. Equivalent weapon positions might hold Japanese railguns, Italian OTO Melara 76 mm guns, or British DragonFire lasers. These are illustrative fits, with different hulls, superstructures, and missile arrangements still expected.

evidence.note: Possible future weapons and an illustrative helicopter and rotary-UAV complement create shared hangar and flight-deck requirements.
Radar familiarity and support costs, with possible Japanese railgun, Italian 76 mm, and British DragonFire fits served by a command system.

segments.summary: Shared helicopters and rotary drones may create similar hangars, while national choices in radar, railguns, lasers, and close-in weapons keep the combat fits distinct.

segments.title: Order volume and requirements in NF-90 and Horizon
segments.body: Order volume connects national requirements with industrial work shares in the NF-90 and Horizon examples. Britain and the United States are said to have accounted at several points for more than two-thirds of NF-90's proposed ships. British requirements reflected Falklands experience, while the American aims included succeeding the Oliver Hazard Perry class and complementing the incoming Burke fleet. Smaller participants are described as feeling that their requirements received less attention. In Horizon, the comparison is twelve planned British ships against four each for France and Italy, with disputes over the firms doing the work and ownership of patents. These examples underpin the source's distinction between American participation in systems research and participation in the proposed hull program. The explanation concerns order size and different national needs, rather than hostility between partners.

evidence.note: NF-90 order shares and differing British and American requirements illustrate the effect of customer scale on a common design.
Horizon order proportions and industrial and patent disputes underpin the distinction between US research and hull-program participation.

segments.summary: NF-90 order shares, Falklands-driven British requirements, and Horizon work-share disputes illustrate national influence on a common ship design.

segments.title: The Defence Investment Plan and procurement funding
segments.body: The closing feasibility critique focuses on the delayed British Defence Investment Plan. Its stated purpose is to connect the Strategic Defence Review's equipment plans with spending. Other reports are described as waiting for its release, with the release date still unknown. The alternatives considered include raising resources to fund the plans, acknowledging that some promises cannot be delivered, and discussing program choices with allies. The passage attributes the delay to the political difficulty of those decisions. That explanation is an interpretation of the delay, rather than an announced reason from the government.

evidence.note: The Defence Investment Plan's funding purpose, other reports awaiting its release, and an interpretation of the political choices surrounding the delay.

segments.summary: The delayed Defence Investment Plan is discussed as the link between announced equipment plans, available funding, and conversations with allies.

segments.title: Drones extend artillery observation
segments.body: The warning against indecision leads to a brief explanation of why remaining stationary is dangerous. Drones have multiplied the effect of forward artillery observers by finding and tracking targets. In this account, artillery still delivers much of the destructive force once the position is known. The distinction separates the sensor from the weapon and shows how uncrewed aircraft strengthen an existing fire-support system.

evidence.note: Stationary targets, drones locating positions, and artillery delivering the destructive effect in the forward-observation analogy.

segments.summary: A short battlefield analogy separates the reconnaissance role of drones from the artillery that strikes a fixed target.

segments.title: Post-Cold War indecision accumulated damage
segments.body: The closing critique attributes accumulated procurement and infrastructure problems across many nations to deferred decisions since the end of the Cold War. Its chronology starts in the early 1990s. Later explanations involving social spending, immigration, or Brexit are rejected on the grounds that the problems predate their prominence in the political debate described here. The conclusion assigns the obstacle to government decisions while expressing confidence in the technical systems and personnel. This is a historical and political interpretation of the proposed program's feasibility.

evidence.note: An interpretation linking problems since the early 1990s to deferred decisions, while expressing confidence in the technical systems and personnel.

segments.summary: Many governments are blamed for deferring military choices since the early 1990s, allowing procurement and infrastructure problems to accumulate.

segments.title: Burke architecture is reaching its design ceiling
segments.body: The Burke's underlying architecture is traced here through 1960s concepts and 1970s development principles into an arrangement established in the 1980s. Repeated modernization has changed the ship without removing that basic framework. Japanese development of the design supplies an example of extensive improvement alongside an expected need for a newer arrangement. The account acknowledges substantial work during the Burke production restart. It also describes caution about changing the design so far that it would be treated as a different ship. The Super Hornet returns as an analogy for a substantially new aircraft that retains a familiar appearance and name.

evidence.note: Japanese developments of the Burke and the argument that upgrades retain an underlying framework from Cold War design concepts.
Caution during the Burke restart, compared with the Super Hornet's familiar appearance despite extensive redesign.

segments.summary: The Burke architecture discussion distinguishes repeated upgrades from replacement of the underlying ship design and returns to the Super Hornet analogy.

segments.title: Shared systems with nationally tailored ships
segments.body: The final proposal centers on joint development of systems and weapons. Each country would retain responsibility for its ship and adapt it to national needs. Type 26 is used as an example of related designs with shared features and visible differences. National ownership is part of the argument because each ship would remain the product of the country building it. The qualified conclusion supports the proposed cooperation at the systems level while leaving hull designs distinct.

evidence.note: The proposed division between joint systems development and national ship ownership, using Type 26's similarities and differences as an example.

segments.summary: Type 26 supplies the concluding example of related ships retaining national differences within the proposed systems partnership.

segments.title: An LPD could tend uncrewed missile vessels
segments.body: An alternative concept uses an LPD-like command ship with docking space for uncrewed missile vessels. The craft could come aboard to rearm and then return to patrol, while the command ship carries weapons of its own. This would replace the long return journey to a home port with replenishment from a ship accompanying the force. A supply ship would still have to deliver ammunition and other stores to the tender. The proposed hull volume is connected with room to handle VLS reloading at sea, though the number of uncrewed craft and supporting helicopters remains to be worked out. The San Antonio-derived cruiser idea supplies an example of the missile capacity available in an LPD hull. The concept is described as a large and complicated option.

evidence.note: An LPD-like armed command ship with docking and reloading space for uncrewed missile vessels, replenished by a supply ship.
Unresolved numbers of uncrewed vessels and helicopters, the concept's complexity, and missile capacity in a San Antonio-derived hull.

segments.summary: A large command-and-support ship with a well deck offers one way to rearm and control distributed missile vessels without sending every empty unit home.
